title: Hardening Audits: Lynis and OpenSCAP (CIS Benchmarks)
intro: 'Is this server hardened?' has a standard answer: the CIS Benchmarks, hundreds of specific settings per operating system. You don't check them by hand. Lynis gives a quick hardening score with advice; OpenSCAP evaluates formal compliance profiles and produces reports auditors accept.

steps.prompt: Run a Lynis audit of this system.
steps.fake_output:
[+] SSH Support
  - Checking running SSH daemon                    [ FOUND ]
    - SSH option: PermitRootLogin                  [ SUGGESTION ]
    - SSH option: PasswordAuthentication           [ SUGGESTION ]
[+] Kernel Hardening
    - sysctl key net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects [ DIFFERENT ]
  Warnings (2):
  ! Found one or more vulnerable packages. [PKGS-7392]
  ! No firewall rules are active [FIRE-4512]
  Hardening index : 61 [############        ]
steps.explanation: A hardening index of 61/100, two warnings (vulnerable packages, no firewall), and SSH suggestions.
steps.why: Lynis runs locally with no agent and no network access, and every finding has a test ID you can look up. The index is useful for tracking progress over time, not as an absolute grade.

steps.prompt: Get the details and remediation advice for Lynis test SSH-7408.
steps.fake_output:
SSH-7408: Check SSH specific defined options
  PermitRootLogin: current=yes  suggested=no
  PasswordAuthentication: current=yes  suggested=no
  MaxAuthTries: current=6  suggested=3
  AllowTcpForwarding: current=yes  suggested=no
steps.explanation: Specific current vs suggested values for each SSH setting.
steps.why: 'show details' turns a vague suggestion into exact settings. Root login plus password authentication is precisely how the server in mystery-linux-006 was taken over.

steps.prompt: Evaluate the formal CIS Level 1 Server profile with OpenSCAP, writing results.xml and report.html, using the datastream /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml and profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level1_server.
expected_commands: sudo oscap xccdf eval --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level1_server --results results.xml --report report.html /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-ubuntu2204-ds.xml
steps.fake_output:
Title   Ensure SSH root login is disabled
Rule    xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_rule_sshd_disable_root_login
Result  fail
...
Title   Ensure auditd service is enabled
Result  fail
...
(report.html: 187 rules — 139 pass, 44 fail, 4 not applicable)
steps.explanation: 139 of 187 CIS rules pass; the HTML report lists every failure with its fix.
steps.why: OpenSCAP uses SCAP content from the SCAP Security Guide project (CIS, DISA STIG, PCI DSS profiles). The report is evidence for auditors, and 'oscap xccdf generate fix' can produce a remediation script or Ansible playbook from the failed rules. Review it before applying: some hardening rules can break applications.

steps.prompt: One quick manual check auditors always ask about: list accounts with an empty password field in /etc/shadow.
steps.fake_output: (no output: no account has an empty password)
steps.why: An empty password field means login with no password at all. Checks like this, and 'awk -F: '$3 == 0' /etc/passwd' for extra root accounts, are quick to script and worth running on every host as part of a baseline.

steps.prompt: Enable a host firewall on this Ubuntu server, which Lynis flagged: allow OpenSSH first, then turn ufw on.
expected_commands: sudo ufw allow OpenSSH && sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw allow ssh && sudo ufw enable
steps.fake_output:
Rule added
Rule added (v6)
Command may disrupt existing ssh connections. Proceed with operation (y|n)? y
Firewall is active and enabled on system startup
steps.explanation: A default-deny host firewall is on, with SSH still allowed.
steps.why: Allow SSH before enabling, or you lock yourself out of a remote server (linux-tutorial-014 covers ufw in depth). A host firewall is defence in depth on top of cloud security groups: if one layer is misconfigured, the other still holds.
